books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Minority report, Senate Select Committee to Investigate the Causes of the Removal of the Negroes from the Southern States to the Northern States, Senate Report 693 (1880)

stimulus.text:
“In the spring of 1879, thousands of colored people, unable longer to endure the intolerable hardships, injustice, and suffering inflicted upon them by a class of Democrats in the South, had, in utter despair, fled panic-stricken from their homes and sought protection among strangers in a strange land. Homeless, penniless, and in rags, these poor people were thronging the wharves of Saint Louis, crowding the steamers on the Mississippi River, and in pitiable destitution throwing themselves upon the charity of Kansas.”

—Minority report, Senate Select Committee to Investigate the Causes of the Removal of the Negroes from the Southern States to the Northern States, 1880
stimulus.source_note: Minority report of the Senate Select Committee investigating the Negro Exodus, Senate Report 693, 46th Congress, 2nd Session (1880). Public domain (congressional report; text verified against the National Archives, “Exodus to Kansas,” Prologue, Summer 2008).

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: According to the report, the Exodusters left the South mainly because

options.text: the federal government offered them free land in Kansas.
options.misconception: Background: the government offered no such program; migrants went on their own, hoping to homestead.

options.text: Kansas factories were hiring thousands of workers.
options.misconception: Background: Kansas offered farmland, not factory jobs; most Exodusters hoped to farm.

options.text: they could no longer endure violence and injustice in the South.
the Supreme Court had ordered Southern states to pay them damages.
options.misconception: Background: the Court issued no such order; it narrowed Black rights instead.

rationales.A: Background: the government offered no such program; migrants went on their own, hoping to homestead.
rationales.B: Background: Kansas offered farmland, not factory jobs; most Exodusters hoped to farm.
rationales.C: The report says they fled “in utter despair” from “intolerable hardships, injustice, and suffering.” They were not pulled west by a promise; they were pushed out by what the South had become after Reconstruction’s end.
rationales.D: Background: the Court issued no such order; it narrowed Black rights instead.
rationales.general:
1. The report’s first words name the cause: hardships, injustice, and suffering they could no longer endure.
2. The migrants fled “in utter despair” and “panic-stricken,” the words of people escaping, not of people choosing.
3. They arrived homeless, penniless, and in rags, which shows no one had paid their way.
4. Kansas was the refuge, but the South’s violence was the reason.
Remember: when people flee in rags, ask what they were fleeing, not what they were promised.
